> **[case-study]**
> **Perrin Storage**
> 
> Perrin Storage operates refrigerated warehouses in country M, storing frozen food for producers and supermarkets.
> 
> **Table 1: Perrin Storage data**
> 
> |   | **2024** | **2025** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Capacity utilisation (%) | 91 | 98 |
> | Storage requests refused (pallets) | 2 400 | 9 100 |
> | Energy cost as % of total costs | 34 | 41 |
> | Equipment breakdowns per year | 7 | 19 |
> 
> Perrin Storage is considering building a third warehouse at a cost of \$4.2 million. It would take 18 months to complete and increase total capacity by 45%.
> 
> The Operations Director, Elena Vasquez, argues the business is turning away too much work, and that breakdowns have risen because the existing refrigeration plant runs continuously with no time for maintenance.
> 
> The Finance Director, Hugo Bram, is cautious. Two of Perrin Storage's three largest customers are on contracts due for renewal within two years, and a competitor has announced its own new facility 30 km away.

Evaluate whether Perrin Storage should build the third warehouse.
parts.solution_md:
Operating close to or above maximum capacity means a business has little or no slack in its resources **[K]**. Perrin Storage's utilisation has risen from 91% to 98%, and refused storage requests have almost quadrupled from 2 400 to 9 100 pallets **[Ap]**. That refused business is revenue going directly to competitors, and customers turned away once may not return **[An]**. Breakdowns have also risen from 7 to 19 a year because refrigeration plant runs continuously with no maintenance window, and in cold storage a breakdown risks the customer's stock rather than merely delaying it **[An]**

However, \$4.2 million is a large commitment against uncertain demand **[Ap]**. A competitor is opening a facility 30 km away, which may absorb precisely the demand Perrin Storage is currently refusing **[An]**. Two of its three largest customers are also up for renewal within two years, so a substantial share of existing demand is not secure either; the warehouse could open into a market that has both gained a competitor and lost a major customer **[An]**

Overall, the operational case is stronger than the demand case **[E]**. Rising breakdowns are a present and worsening cost that will damage customer relationships whether or not demand grows, so some investment in capacity or maintenance capability is needed regardless **[E]**. The demand justification, by contrast, rests on refused pallets that a nearby competitor may shortly be able to serve **[E]**. Perrin Storage should therefore secure renewal of its two major contracts before committing, and consider a smaller facility that relieves the maintenance problem without betting \$4.2 million on demand it may not hold once the competitor opens **[E]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Whitlow**
> 
> Whitlow is a commercial laundry in country F, washing linen for restaurants, care homes and gyms. It operates two sites.
> 
> **Table 1: Whitlow site data, 2025**
> 
> |   | **Site A (Elmhurst)** | **Site B (Portway)** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Maximum capacity (tonnes of linen per week) | 90 | 60 |
> | Actual output (tonnes per week) | 74 | 26 |
> | Capacity utilisation (%) | 82 | 43 |
> | Fixed costs per week (\$) | 11 000 | 9 500 |
> | Distance from Site A (km) | - | 55 |
> 
> Site B opened four years ago to serve a growing hotel market, but two large hotel customers have since closed. Site B employs 14 people, several of whom have been with Whitlow since it opened.
> 
> The Operations Director, Sam Reilly, proposes closing Site B and transferring its work to Site A, which has spare capacity.
> 
> The Managing Director, Nadia Okonjo, is reluctant. Site B's remaining customers are all within 20 km of Portway and may not accept longer delivery times from Elmhurst. She also notes that a new business park near Portway is due to open next year.

Evaluate whether Whitlow should close Site B in order to improve its capacity utilisation.
parts.solution_md:
Capacity utilisation is the proportion of maximum possible output a business is actually producing **[K]**. Site B runs at only 43% while carrying fixed costs of \$9 500 a week **[Ap]**. Closing it would remove those fixed costs entirely and concentrate output at Site A, raising utilisation there and lowering the average cost per tonne across the business **[An]**. Since Site B's under-utilisation is caused by customers who have permanently closed rather than by a temporary dip, waiting for that capacity to fill again may simply prolong the loss **[An]**

However, the proposal does not work as stated **[Ap]**. Site A has maximum capacity of 90 tonnes and already produces 74, leaving only 16 tonnes spare, whereas Site B handles 26 tonnes **[An]**. Transferring all the work would exceed Site A's capacity by 10 tonnes a week, so Whitlow would either have to invest in expanding Site A or turn away roughly 40% of Site B's business, losing the revenue that closure was meant to protect **[An]**

Overall, Whitlow should not close Site B on the terms proposed **[E]**. The financial logic is sound in principle, but it rests on an assumption about spare capacity that the figures contradict, and a decision that costs 10 tonnes of weekly business is not a saving **[E]**. The customers within 20 km of Portway compound this, since some would likely leave rather than accept a 55 km delivery distance **[E]**. Whitlow should instead pursue customers from the new business park to fill Site B, and revisit closure in twelve months if utilisation has not improved, by which point it would also know whether expanding Site A is affordable **[E]**

> - Whitlow could close Site B and transfer its work to Site A. However, Site A has only 16 tonnes of spare capacity against Site B's 26, so the transfer as proposed would exceed Site A's capacity by 10 tonnes a week

>

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ashmore Glass**
> 
> Ashmore Glass manufactures glass bottles and jars in country R, supplying drinks producers and food manufacturers. It operates its own fleet of 22 lorries and employs 34 drivers.
> 
> **Table 1: Ashmore Glass distribution data**
> 
> |   | **2023** | **2025** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Distribution cost as % of revenue | 8.1 | 11.4 |
> | Average lorry utilisation per journey (%) | 71 | 58 |
> | Deliveries made on the agreed date (%) | 96 | 94 |
> | Number of drivers | 30 | 34 |
> 
> A national logistics company has offered to take over all of Ashmore Glass's distribution for a fixed fee equivalent to 8.5% of revenue. It would guarantee delivery within two days, but not on a specified date. Ashmore Glass would sell its lorries, and the 34 drivers would be made redundant.
> 
> The Finance Director, Priya Nadar, argues the offer would cut distribution costs immediately and release the capital tied up in an increasingly underused fleet.
> 
> The Sales Director, Tom Ackley, disagrees. Several of Ashmore Glass's largest customers run just-in-time production and specify exact delivery dates, and he believes recent contracts were won partly on the company's on-time record. He also questions whether an outside provider would handle fragile glass as carefully.
> 
> Ashmore Glass must respond within a month.

Evaluate whether Ashmore Glass should outsource its distribution to the national logistics company.
parts.solution_md:
Outsourcing means paying another business to carry out an activity previously done in-house **[K]**. Ashmore Glass's distribution costs have risen from 8.1% to 11.4% of revenue, while the logistics company would charge 8.5% **[Ap]**. That is an immediate saving of almost three percentage points of revenue, and it removes a cost that has been rising steeply **[An]**. Lorry utilisation has also fallen to 58%, so Ashmore Glass is running half-empty vehicles; a national operator combining loads across many clients would not, which is precisely why it can charge less **[An]**

However, the provider guarantees delivery only within two days, not on a specified date **[Ap]**. Customers running just-in-time production hold almost no inventory, so a delivery arriving a day early or late is a serious problem for them rather than a minor inconvenience **[An]**. If those customers are among the largest, losing even one could cost more revenue than the 2.9 percentage points saved on distribution **[An]**

Overall, whether Ashmore Glass should outsource depends on whether the date problem can be solved rather than on the cost saving **[E]**. The saving is certain, immediate and addresses a genuine deterioration, so doing nothing is not attractive either **[E]**. The risk, though, is concentrated in a few large JIT customers, and concentrated risks are exactly the ones that damage a business badly rather than gradually **[E]**. Ashmore Glass should therefore treat guaranteed delivery dates for its JIT customers as a condition of the contract, and if the provider will not agree, outsource only its general deliveries while retaining a small fleet for those accounts **[E]**

> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Ashmore Glass could outsource all distribution to the logistics company. Distribution costs have risen from 8.1% to 11.4% of revenue against a fixed offer of 8.5%, and lorry utilisation has fallen to 58%, so a national operator consolidating loads across many clients can carry the work more cheaply than Ashmore Glass can itself. However, a smaller fleet would have even worse utilisation than 58% and higher cost per journey, so the saving would be materially reduced
> - Making 34 drivers redundant carries redundancy costs and would damage morale among remaining employees. However, the alternative is continuing to run a fleet whose utilisation is falling and whose costs are rising faster than revenue
>

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** impact of outsourcing on a business.
parts.solution_md:
Outsourcing is when a business pays another business to carry out an activity it would otherwise perform itself **[1]**. The specialist provider often produces at lower cost because it operates on a larger scale across many clients, so the business's own costs fall **[1]**. However, the business no longer controls that activity directly, so if the provider's quality slips or it delivers late, the business must answer to its own customers for a failure it did not cause and cannot immediately fix **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Outsourcing means paying an external business to carry out an activity previously done in-house
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Specialist providers operating at scale can perform the activity more cheaply than the business itself
> - Outsourcing frees management time and capital to focus on the core activity
> - Direct control over quality and timing is lost, and problems take longer to correct
> - The business remains accountable to its own customers for work it no longer performs
> - Redundancies among staff who previously did the work can damage morale among those remaining
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The saving and the loss of control are two sides of the same decision: the work is cheaper precisely because someone else is now doing it. Strong answers make that connection explicit rather than treating cost and control as unrelated points. Follow the consequence through to the customer, who still holds the business responsible.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** method a business could use to improve its capacity utilisation.
parts.solution_md:
Capacity utilisation can be improved either by raising output or by reducing the maximum capacity available **[1]**. One method is to rent out unused premises or equipment to another business **[1]**. This generates income from resources that would otherwise sit idle and reduces the effective capacity the business is measured against, so utilisation rises without the business needing to find extra demand of its own **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Capacity utilisation improves when output rises relative to maximum capacity, or when maximum capacity falls
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Renting out spare premises or equipment earns income from idle assets and reduces effective capacity
> - Promotional activity or price reductions can raise demand and therefore output
> - Producing under another firm's brand name fills spare capacity without competing with existing sales
> - Rationalisation, such as closing one site, cuts maximum capacity so the remaining sites run fuller
> - Subcontracting work in from other businesses uses spare capacity during quiet periods
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> There are two routes to better capacity utilisation and most answers only ever use one. Raising output is the obvious one; reducing capacity is the other, and it is often the realistic choice when demand simply is not there. Showing you know both directions exist is a quick way to stand out.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** problem for a business of operating over maximum capacity.
parts.solution_md:
Operating over maximum capacity means a business is producing beyond the level its resources are designed to sustain **[1]**. Machinery is run for longer without maintenance and staff work extended hours, which increases the risk of breakdowns, fatigue and mistakes **[1]**. Defective output must then be scrapped or reworked, which adds cost and can mean orders are delivered late, damaging the business's reputation with the very customers whose extra demand caused the pressure **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Operating over maximum capacity means producing beyond the level resources can sustain
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Machinery run without maintenance breaks down more often, halting production entirely
> - Staff working extended hours become fatigued, so error rates and accidents rise
> - Reworking or scrapping defective output adds cost and consumes further capacity
> - Late delivery damages relationships with customers gained during a period of high demand
> - Overtime payments raise labour costs per unit even though output has increased
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Operating at full capacity and operating over it are different situations, and only one of them is a problem. At full capacity a business is efficient but inflexible; beyond it, resources are being pushed past what they can sustain. Make clear in your first sentence which of the two you are writing about.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** impact on employees of a business operating under maximum capacity.
parts.solution_md:
Operating under maximum capacity means a business is producing below the level its resources allow **[1]**. If this continues, the business may not need all of its workforce, so employees may face reduced hours or redundancy **[1]**. The resulting uncertainty can lower motivation and prompt the most employable staff to leave for more secure work, so the business loses experienced workers it will need again once demand recovers **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Operating under maximum capacity means output is below what the business's resources could produce
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Reduced hours or redundancies become likely if under-utilisation persists
> - Job insecurity lowers motivation and productivity among remaining staff
> - The most employable workers leave first, so the business loses its strongest people
> - Recruiting and retraining when demand recovers is costly and slow
> - Quieter periods do allow time for training or maintenance that a busy business cannot fit in
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks for an impact, check whether it has specified on whom. Costs and profit are the reflex answer, but this one names employees, so an answer about unit costs earns nothing however well argued. Read the last few words of the stem before you start writing.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** impact on a business of operating under maximum capacity.
parts.solution_md:
Operating under maximum capacity means a business is producing less than it could with its existing resources **[1]**. Its fixed costs, such as rent, insurance and management salaries, do not fall when output falls, so those costs are spread across fewer units **[1]**. This raises the fixed cost per unit, which either reduces the profit made on each item sold or forces the business to raise its price and risk losing customers to competitors producing at fuller capacity **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Operating under maximum capacity means producing below the level the business's resources allow
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Fixed costs are unchanged by output, so spreading them over fewer units raises average cost per unit
> - Higher unit costs squeeze profit margins or force a price rise that weakens competitiveness
> - Machinery and premises stand idle, so capital is tied up in assets that are not earning
> - Spare capacity does allow the business to accept a sudden large order without disruption
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mechanism here is that fixed costs do not shrink when output does. Answers saying costs "go up" without explaining why rarely reach the third mark. Name the fixed costs, point out that they continue regardless, and the rise in cost per unit follows logically.

Outsourcing is when a business pays another business to carry out an activity **[1]** that it would otherwise have performed itself **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Outsourcing is the transfer of a business function, such as production, distribution or customer service, to an external provider
> - Outsourcing means contracting an outside specialist to do work previously done in-house
> - Outsourcing is the practice of buying in a service or component from another business rather than producing it internally

> **[exam-tip]**
> An outsourcing definition needs two parties: the business handing the work over and the one taking it on. Saying a business "gets work done elsewhere" leaves out the crucial point that it used to do that work itself. That contrast is what separates outsourcing from ordinary buying.

Capacity utilisation is the proportion of a business's maximum possible output that it is currently producing **[1]**, usually expressed as a percentage **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Capacity utilisation measures actual output as a percentage of the maximum output a business could achieve with its existing resources
> - Capacity utilisation shows how fully a business is using its available premises, machinery and workforce
> - Capacity utilisation is the ratio of current output to maximum possible output, expressed as a percentage

> **[exam-tip]**
> Capacity utilisation is a comparison, so a definition mentioning only what a business produces has left out the half that matters. The figure only means anything against the maximum the business could produce. Get both quantities into your sentence and the percentage explains itself.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** implication for a business of operating at full capacity.
parts.solution_md:
One implication for a business of operating at full capacity is that it is unable to increase output to meet any extra demand **[1]**. Since the business is already producing the maximum amount possible with its current resources, it cannot fulfil unexpected orders or a sudden rise in customer demand. This could mean the business has to turn potential customers away, resulting in lost sales that it cannot recover **[1]**. If this happens regularly, customers may become frustrated and take their business to a competitor instead, which could damage the business's reputation and reduce its future sales **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Unable to increase output to meet additional demand.
> - Risk of overstretching resources, leading to quality problems.
> - Opportunity to maximise revenue and spread fixed costs over maximum output.
> - May need to consider expanding capacity.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Unable to meet additional demand because the business is producing at its maximum, it cannot fulfil unexpected orders or increases in demand without turning customers away, which may result in lost sales and could damage relationships with customers who take their custom elsewhere.
> - Risk of overstretching resources - pushing machinery and staff to their limit for a sustained period increases the risk of breakdowns, staff fatigue or errors, which could lead to a fall in the quality of output and increased costs from reworking or rejected items.
> - Maximises revenue/spreads fixed costs because fixed costs are spread across the maximum possible number of units produced, operating at full capacity lowers the average fixed cost per unit, which can increase profitability; however, this leaves no spare capacity if demand rises further.
> - May need to expand capacity - consistently operating at full capacity may signal that current demand exceeds what the business can supply, so it may need to invest in additional capacity, such as new machinery or premises, to avoid permanently losing sales to competitors.
> 
> Accept any other valid response

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students lose marks by listing several implications rather than fully developing one. The command word "explain" means you need to go beyond identification - show the chain of reasoning by linking the implication to its effect on the business. A useful structure is: state the implication, then use connective phrases such as "this means that..." or "as a result..." to build your explanation. Make sure your explanation clearly relates back to the concept of full capacity, not just general business issues.

**[3 marks]**

**Fashion Frames plc (FF) **

FF makes plastic frames for glasses (spectacles) in a factory in country W, in South East Asia. FF sells its plastic frames to wholesale businesses that market well-known brands of plastic frames which they sell globally. The wholesalers reject 7% of the frames supplied by FF because of substandard quality. The FF design team create dynamic styles based on the demands of the wholesalers. Meeting delivery times is very important. FF only delivers 85% of its sales on time. FF needs to improve this percentage. Improving quality Chang, the production manager, aims to reduce the high level of rejects by the wholesalers. He has identified a number of factors which make this difficult including: • employees know that rejected frames can be recycled • production targets are very difficult to meet • problems with suppliers of raw materials • breakdowns with machinery. Chang proposes introducing Total Quality Management (TQM). He thinks this will reduce the number of substandard frames and improve FF’s delivery times. Chang forecasts successful implementation of TQM will also increase output by 10% and average variable cost will fall by 5%. However, Chang is aware that there may be problems with TQM and forecasts can be inaccurate. Table 1 shows information on FF’s output, costs and prices, before TQM is implemented. Table 1: FF’s output, costs and prices Year ending September 2021 Maximum capacity 16 million frames Actual output 14 million frames Average variable cost \$20 Average selling price \$40 Communication challenges FF has a centralised organisational structure with a low degree of delegation. Directors make decisions, department managers plan how to implement these and supervisors give instructions. Employees have little responsibility or control. FF has provided good pay, good conditions of work and security of employment. However, employees are aware that the directors are considering significant changes to working conditions. All employees find it difficult to discuss this with their line managers. Many employees work alone so information is passed on informally and often inaccurately. This uncertainty has begun to lead to dissatisfaction, complaints, higher absence rates and lower productivity. Privatisation of electricity and water industries In country W, state-owned businesses supply all electricity and water. Prices of services in these industries have risen at above the rate of inflation for the last three years. Sometimes, electricity supply is interrupted and FF finds it difficult to obtain information about reconnection. Water quality is variable. The government has announced it intends to privatise these industries in the next three years, to improve these services.

Buying 3D printers 3D printers that make frames for glasses as part of a CAD/CAM process are becoming available. There is no way of accurately estimating their value after four years. The directors have told Chang that an acceptable accounting rate of return (ARR) is 5%. Chang thinks new 3D printers will increase FF’s long-term profitability. The 3D printers will result in significant reductions in employee costs and waste and substandard reject costs. Maintenance and training costs will, however, increase. Table 2 and Table 3 show some of Chang’s research. He knows competitors are considering buying them. Product development and marketing The marketing manager is concerned that FF relies only on specific orders from wholesalers for plastic frames. He proposes that FF should use product development to design and manufacture metal glasses frames. These would be marketed to wholesalers and directly to businesses who sell glasses with globally recognised brands. FF would have to acquire new skills and equipment in order to design and manufacture metal frames. The marketing manager visited international trade fairs and found that several competitors have research and development (R&D) departments. Strategic choice: enter the Asia Pacific retail market The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) states: ‘My strategic analysis shows that FF must continue with the current business model but should take a new direction as well. My strategic choice is that FF should enter the retail glasses market in the Asia Pacific region. This will mean selling our own glasses in retail shops. We will need to work closely with lens manufacturers. Increased eye strain and higher disposable income are driving the increasing demand for higher value glasses. We could use the Ansoff Matrix to help analyse the link between this business strategy and risk. There are several approaches we could use to enter this new market.’

The CEO illustrates his proposal with Table 4 and Table 5. Employees only carry out the one task they have been trained for in the production process. The Directors are considering a proposal from Chang to move to team working. **Thierry’s Kitchen (TK) **

Thierry’s Kitchen (TK) operates in four European countries with its head office in country H. TK was started by Thierry Radelet in 2017, after he gave up a senior management role in a food delivery company to start his own business. Thierry had observed the rise in popularity of delivery of cooked meals to offices and households. He identified a gap in the market for an efficient service, which would focus on high‑quality cooked meals for delivery only. TK grew quickly and converted to a public limited company in 2019. TK now has two kitchens in each of four European capital cities. The eight locations are outside the city centres and each kitchen has the capacity to produce 2200 meals each day. Meals are packaged and then delivered to customers by motorcycle. Thierry works at the company’s head office, attached to TK’s first kitchen location in country H. He visits the other kitchens once every month. Thierry and a team of directors make all the major decisions about the main menu items and new locations. Each kitchen has a manager who is responsible for decisions about inventory management and human resources. TK has financed its growth through retained profits and a loan of \$15 million. Dividend payments to shareholders have been consistently above average for the catering industry. External environment The European countries in which TK operates experienced economic recessions during 2020. There has been economic growth since then. Governments have supported recovering economies with grants and loans to small and medium‑sized businesses, including TK. Social and technological changes have included fewer consumers eating at restaurants. Smartphone apps are increasingly used for online shopping and ordering meal deliveries. More employees are now working from home rather than in offices. The populations of European capital cities include significant numbers of young, professional individuals who earn above average incomes. Marketing TK differentiates its meal service from the increasing number of competitors on the basis of choice, quality and packaging. The menu is varied and includes daily special offers. Consumers are assured of the high‑quality of TK’s meals as it provides a complete service; from sourcing ingredients to cooking, packaging and delivery. TK’s Operations Director has worked closely with a packaging company to research, develop and patent a range of recyclable packaging containers that ensure meals arrive hot and in excellent condition. Marketing is mainly on its website and social media. However, TK’s Marketing Director believes that the monthly distribution of leaflets to businesses and households is a good use of the marketing budget. The average selling price of a meal is \$8. The delivery charge is \$5 per order and the average order is for 3 meals. Innovation Thierry has always ensured that TK is at the forefront of product and process innovations in the food delivery business. The majority of TK’s orders are received through its smartphone app. Thierry and the other TK directors are now interested in trialling automated (driverless) delivery vehicles (ADVs) in country H. The ADVs will be computer controlled and offer fast, low‑cost meal deliveries. ADVs may be ideal for deliveries in city locations. The capital cost of the ADV trial will be \$1.5 million. This could be financed by further bank borrowing or a new share issue.

Operations and human resources TK’s kitchen operations are labour‑intensive. Meals are produced using batch production, but demand for different meals is difficult to predict due to changing food trends. This makes it very difficult to control inventory. Frequently, too much of some menu items is produced leading to food wastage. Recently, following a social media review praising a TK vegan curry meal, demand increased so quickly that the kitchens failed to produce enough. Some customers were disappointed because their orders were not met. TK’s Operations Director is investigating the use of lean production techniques, such as Just in Time (JIT), which he believes could improve efficiency. Each kitchen employs a manager and a team of ten full‑time chefs on permanent employment contracts. There are also kitchen assistants, meal packers and delivery drivers who are employed on a range of part‑time and zero‑hours contracts. Workers are under pressure to constantly improve productivity while maintaining high quality. As Thierry always reminds employees ‘the quality of our food is our USP, because we do not see customers face‑to‑face or serve them their meals’. Most TK employees are shareholders in the company. Annual productivity bonuses are paid in TK shares. Kitchen 2 – a problem kitchen Kitchen 2 is one of TK’s kitchens in country J. HD designs and manufactures micro circuit boards containing advanced software. The boards are used in data processing, IT system manufacture and vehicle control. HD is a private limited company with two shareholders who are also the directors. One is responsible for the Design Division, the other for the Manufacturing Division. HD started in 2002 and now employs 18 electronic engineering graduates. One of these graduates is responsible for managing HD’s website and for dealing with customer enquiries and orders. HD also employs an accountant and two administration staff. HD is located in country Q. HD still has its original mission statement: “to provide world class software solutions to customers”. The geographic split of HD’s sales is: • 40% country Q • 30% US • 30% other countries Corporate social responsibility (CSR) issues HD’s customers include social media operators, police and security forces, retailers, governments and universities. The micro circuit boards contain metals, such as nickel, which are difficult to recycle. Some pressure groups claim that metals used in micro circuit boards are obtained from mines which employ child labour. HD’s accountant also believes that some manufacturers make payments to foreign governments which do not appear in their company accounts. Two pressure groups and country Q’s government have asked HD for a detailed social audit. Organisational structure The Design Division is organised in a matrix structure. Design engineers work on their own and also in small teams, each on a specific project such as a customer’s special order. These temporary teams exist for the life of each custom made circuit board project. Each team has designers with the particular skills required. The Design Director delegates responsibility to each team for the completion of each project. The teams choose their own leaders and a team member to communicate with the customer. HD design engineers work from home for 20% of their hours. They communicate by electronic methods except when a team holds problem‑solving meetings. HD’s project design teams have an excellent reputation with customers for designing problem‑ free circuit boards to meet their specific needs. However, the Design Director is worried about recent trends in the Design Division. Absenteeism and labour turnover of design engineers are increasing and project completion dates are being delayed. One design engineer told the director “I have two managers to report to and working with constantly changing teams is bad for morale”. See Table 1 for human resources data.
